question: to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) Subject:

Despite Parliament’s resolution of 16 September 2021 on a coordinated EU action plan to accelerate the transition to innovation without the use of animals in research, regulatory testing and education, there have been multiple reports indicating that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is continuing under the current regulatory framework. While the Cosmetic Products Regulation ((EC) No 1223/2009) establishes a clear ban on animal testing for cosmetic products and ingredients, similar protections do not appear to be applied consistently under the Detergents Regulation ((EC) No 648/2004) and the REACH Regulation ((EC) No 1907/2006) on the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals. Furthermore, Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes requires that animal testing be replaced wherever scientifically satisfactory alternative methods exist. In the light of the EU’s Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, which commits to phasing out animal testing and promoting alternative methods, can the Commission clarify: 1.
How it explains that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is still permitted under the REACH Regulation and related legislation?
What concrete legislative steps and timelines are envisaged to ensure full alignment with Parliament’s resolution and Directive 2010/63/EU?
How it ensures that the European Chemicals Agency systematically prioritises validated non-animal methods and avoids unnecessary testing when evaluating dossiers?
answer: (English version) to the Commission Sebastian Everding (The Left) (11 March 2026) Subject: Animal testing for cleaning products under EU law Despite Parliament’s resolution of 16 September 2021 on a coordinated EU action plan to accelerate the transition to innovation without the use of animals in research, regulatory testing and education, there have been multiple reports indicating that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is continuing under the current regulatory framework. While the Cosmetic Products Regulation ((EC) No 1223/2009) establishes a clear ban on animal testing for cosmetic products and ingredients, similar protections do not appear to be applied consistently under the Detergents Regulation ((EC) No 648/2004) and the REACH Regulation ((EC) No 1907/2006) on the registration, evaluation, authorisation and restriction of chemicals. Furthermore, Directive 2010/63/EU on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes requires that animal testing be replaced wherever scientifically satisfactory alternative methods exist. In the light of the EU’s Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, which commits to phasing out animal testing and promoting alternative methods, can the Commission clarify: 1.
How it explains that the use of animal testing for cleaning products is still permitted under the REACH Regulation and related legislation?
What concrete legislative steps and timelines are envisaged to ensure full alignment with Parliament’s resolution and Directive 2010/63/EU?
How it ensures that the European Chemicals Agency systematically prioritises validated non-animal methods and avoids unnecessary testing when evaluating dossiers?

(29 April 2026) The revised Regulation on Detergents and Surfactants (1), which will enter into force on 23 September 2029, has introduced a general prohibition on the placing on the market of detergents and surfactants that have been subject to animal testing to meet the requirements of the regulation. At the same time, ingredients of cleaning products are subject to the provisions under the regulation on Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) (2) or the Biocidal Product Regulation (3), which might include animal testing if necessary for assessing risks to human health or the environment. Both regulations permit testing on vertebrates only as a last resort. REACH registrants are bound by the principle of last resort when submitting data to the European Chemicals Agency, which is taking this principle into account when evaluating testing proposals or the compliance of dossiers. The principle of last resort aligns these regulations with Directive 2010/63/EU (4), which requires that animal testing be replaced, reduced, or refined, if scientifically possible. The Commission roadmap towards phasing out animal testing for chemical safety assessments, planned to be published in the second quarter of 2026, will outline the steps necessary to reach the goal of phasing out animal testing for chemical safety assessments under all relevant pieces of legislation. Legislative changes, if necessary to reach the goal, will be introduced in line with the rules of the relevant pieces of legislation.
